output.name: Ruskel

anatomy.part: top edge of the wooden knob, the round cap above the handle
the knot where the knob, the T-bar and the shaft join (the brightest star)
the waist of the tapered spike shaft
the point of the spike, where the three rope-opening strands splay out
left end of the T-bar grip
right end of the T-bar grip

output.myth: When Aun cut the string, the rope that held the sky came apart in his hands, and the sky went up with its ends frayed. Mother Hesk sent the Gulls down to say so. Nobody on the islands could splice a rope that long from below, so Ennu the Kite-Wright carved the first Ruskel from bone, thick at the knot and fine at the point, and gave it to the rope-makers. You push the point between the strands, you open a gap, you lay the new strand in and draw it through. Hesk says the same can be done to the sky. So at the rope-making feast the people hold up the Fid, and in autumn it rises over the Lamp Road, pointed at the place where the string was cut. Aun is not there. But the knot of his old tether still shows in the sky if you know where to look, and the Fid is always pointed at it, and never quite reaches.
output.verse:
Open the cut rope
with a bone point, slow and sure,
draw the new strand through.
